  "text": "The first letter arrived three days after we buried my father.

STOP WINDING THE CLOCK.

No signature. Just those five words, written in his cramped capitals.

I assumed it was my brother's idea of a joke. Dad had wound the grandfather clock every Sunday for forty years. Now it stood in my hallway, losing seven minutes a day.

I wound it that evening.

At midnight, something knocked inside the cabinet.

Three polite taps.

I opened the glass door. The pendulum swung. Behind the brass weights, a strip of wallpaper had peeled away.

Our old kitchen wallpaper. Yellow pears.

I sold that house in March.

The second letter came through the slot while I was watching it.

HE CAN ONLY COME AS FAR AS YOU LET THE HANDS GO.

The clock struck one.

From inside came the scrape of a chair across linoleum.

Then my father's voice.

“Help me up, sweetheart.”

I gripped the minute hand and held it still.

The voice stopped. So did the pendulum.

At dawn, my brother answered his phone.

“Dad's clock,” I said. “Did he ever tell you—”

“Don't touch it.”

“I'm holding the hands.”

He began to cry.

Beneath my fingers, the minute hand pushed forward.

“Where's yours?” he asked.

I looked toward the kitchen.

The cheap wall clock above the stove was running backward. Its hands swept past eleven, then ten.

Inside the cabinet, my father laughed.

My brother was shouting now, but I couldn't hear him over the clocks.

Every clock in the house was striking.

All except the one I held.

Behind its glass, a hand settled over mine."
